idiom_name: controller or presenter as supply half; partial rendered with explicit locals as the presentational half (ViewComponent when it needs behaviour)
implementation_notes: Rails' rendering model already separates the halves: the controller action or a presenter object assembles the data, and a partial sees only what is passed to it - `render partial: "cart/lines", locals: { lines: @cart.lines }`, or a collection render that hands each child its own local. What replaces the classic container component is the locals contract: an explicit local is the props interface, and a child that takes only locals can be rendered from a literal in a mailer, a test or a component preview. Where the child needs real behaviour or its own tests, a ViewComponent class (or a plain presenter) takes over the supply half, with the same rule: no stray instance variables inside the presentational template. Hand-wiring a model object is only justified for non-HTTP rendering such as mailers, PDFs or static generation.
code_sketch:
<%# app/views/cart/index.html.erb - supply half assembles what children get %> <%= render partial: "cart/lines", locals: { lines: @cart.lines } %> <%# app/views/cart/_lines.html.erb - presentational half: only its locals %>
    <% Array(lines).each do |line| %>
  • <%= line.sku %> x <%= line.quantity %>
    • <% end %>
pitfalls: Partials happily read controller-assigned instance variables, so a partial that was passed nothing still renders - treat stray instance variables in a presentational template as a defect.
A ViewComponent's sidecar template is bound to the component's own methods; reaching past them into the request or the database from the template reintroduces the coupling.
Fragment caching keyed on a mutable object or a stale timestamp serves removed markup; key the cache on the record's updated_at or version.
